title: Simchat Torah close: the circle
hook: the Torah's last letter and first letter spell lev, heart; the scroll rolls straight on

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses, known face to face, and remembered as our teacher. Your line was face to face. Who did you thank? Today, the Torah's very last word, and what happens right after it. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

On Simchat Torah, synagogues get loud. The scrolls come out of the ark and people dance with them, around and around the room, seven circuits, sometimes spilling out into the street. Children wave flags. Someone who hasn't set foot inside all year is handed a scroll to hold. And in the middle of all that, something quiet and precise happens at the reading table. The last words of the Torah are read aloud. And then, without stopping, the first.
screen: `SCROLLS OUT OF THE ARK.` → `SEVEN CIRCUITS OF DANCING.` → `THE LAST WORDS, THEN THE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy ends with the words in the sight of all Israel; in Hebrew, le'einei kol Yisrael. So the last letter of the whole Torah is the lamed at the end of Yisrael. Genesis begins with bereshit, in the beginning, and its first letter is bet. Put the last letter and the first together, lamed and bet, and they spell lev: heart. Some teachers point this out. The Torah, end joined to beginning, makes a heart. On Simchat Torah, the person honored with reading the end is called the chatan Torah, the bridegroom of the Torah. The one honored with starting again is the chatan Bereshit, the bridegroom of the beginning. The scroll isn't rolled up and put away for a rest. It's rolled straight back to its start, and the same day the reading begins again: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Since day three hundred thirty-two, this path has walked from the plagues in Egypt through the rest of Exodus, through Leviticus and Numbers, and these last weeks through Deuteronomy, Moses' farewell. The forgotten sheaf and the first fruits. Choose life. Write your own. The song, the blessing, the grave no one knows, face to face. Tomorrow a new part of the year begins: the siddur, the prayer book, walked page by page. But the Torah doesn't stop. The end touches the beginning.
screen: `LE'EINEI KOL YISRAEL.` · `LAMED AND BET SPELL LEV.` · `TWO BRIDEGROOMS OF THE TORAH.` · `ROLLED STRAIGHT BACK TO THE START.` · then, large: `THE END TOUCHES THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the last and first verses together. Settle, and breathe. Here is the end of the Torah: Moses' mighty deeds, done in the sight of all Israel. And here is the beginning: in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. Say them one after the other, slowly, with no pause in between. Notice what it's like to finish and start in the same breath. Then think of something in your own life that's ending. Where might it touch a beginning? The bell holds the time.
Lev. Heart — the word spelled when the Torah's last letter and its first letter are joined, on the day the ending touches the beginning.
Your line: the end touches the beginning. Today, when you finish something, start the next small thing right away, without the gap. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: On Simchat Torah, congregations dance with the Torah scrolls in seven circuits (hakafot), read the end of Deuteronomy, and immediately begin Genesis again; the two readers are honored as chatan Torah and chatan Bereshit, and some communities honor women with parallel titles.

notes: Deuteronomy 34:12 ends 'in the sight of all Israel' (le'einei kol Yisrael); paraphrased.
The lamed–bet = lev observation is a widely taught homiletic point; attribute as 'teachers have pointed this out'.
Block D close and look-back over year two's Torah walk (days 332–537: Exodus from Bo through Deuteronomy). Year one covered Genesis and early Exodus.
In Israel, Simchat Torah coincides with Shemini Atzeret; outside Israel it is the following day. Not mentioned in the voice.
Some communities honor women as 'kallat Torah' and 'kallat Bereshit'; mentioned in howItsDone only.
